body:
You're correct that AppPageRouteModule's render() method isn’t directly referenced in app-page.ts or edge-ssr.ts. That’s because the call chain originates deeper in the Next.js internal routing and compilation pipeline.

Where it's actually triggered:

The render() method is called via the handle() method defined in the same module. Here's how it flows:

app-page.ts (in next/src/server/app-render/app-page.ts) imports AppPageRouteModule and instantiates it as part of the route handler setup.

The route handler is passed into Next's request handler pipeline, which in turn calls the handle() method on the route module.

Inside that handle() method, Next.js internally calls:

await this.render()

This is the point where your render() method is triggered — dynamically, based on the routing context.

Why you don’t see it statically in VS Code:
Because render() is dynamically referenced inside the class and not statically called from outside the module, the TypeScript analyzer (like in VS Code) won't show any external references to render().

Debug Tip:
If you want to trace execution, place a console.trace() or use a custom logger inside handle() — it’ll confirm that the call hits render() during requests handled via the app directory.

body:
I’ve run into similar traces when monitoring with Sentry. Most of the time `NextNodeServer.clientComponentLoading` just means the server is waiting to render or hydrate client components. It doesn’t always mean something is broken, but it can highlight slow pages or APIs.  

A couple of things you can try:  

- Check if you’re doing heavy work inside `getServerSideProps` or API routes. Those will show up here if they take too long.  
- If you’re using large client components, consider moving data fetching to the server and passing smaller props down.  
- Enable Next.js profiler locally (`NEXT_RUNTIME_PROFILING=1`) to see where rendering is slow.  
- Also test with `next build && next start` locally — sometimes Vercel cold starts or edge settings make things look slower than they are.  

So basically, use these traces as a signal to look at which routes are slow, then profile those pages or APIs to see if there’s unnecessary blocking work.

body:
Hey @Asna08,

When setting up SharePoint for document management, there are a few common pitfalls that can really trip people up and make the system harder to use or manage. 
One big mistake is not thinking through how your sites, libraries, and metadata will be organized from the start. Instead of piling everything into deep folder trees, it’s way better to use metadata and custom views to keep things easy to find and flexible. Skipping metadata or not enforcing it consistently can make searching a pain. Using content types helps keep document templates and metadata uniform, which makes managing files smoother in the long run. 
Permissions can  also get messy if you don’t plan ahead. Too many exceptions or complicated access rules can cause security headaches or accidentally lock people out. It’s worth spending some time upfront setting clear permission groups and roles. SharePoint has a lot of features and quirks, so without good user training and documentation, adoption tends to lag. Simple guides and some ongoing support can make a big difference. Not turning on versioning or skipping check-out features can cause confusion if people overwrite each other’s work. Make sure version control is enabled and consider requiring check-out for important files.

Also, don’t overlook automation tools like Power Automate. Setting up workflows for approvals or notifications can save tons of manual effort and keep processes consistent.
Lastly, search can be a game-changer if set up right. Take some time to configure managed properties and highlight key documents so people can find what they need without hassle.

### TL;DR
SharePoint works best when you take a bit of time to plan and set things up thoughtfully, especially around metadata, governance, and training. 
If you want, I can share some sample templates or governance ideas to get you started!

body:
Hi @TarekAbdelfatah,

You’re on the right track thinking about SPA-like fallback for offline support with dynamic routes in Next.js 15’s App Router, but this use case is indeed tricky because static pre-caching all dynamic pages is impossible and Next.js’ default static optimizations don’t fully cover this.

### 1. **Conceptual approach: Offline-first with fallback page**

* Since you cannot pre-cache all dynamic routes (e.g., millions of `doc/[id]` pages), the typical pattern is:

  * Pre-cache static assets (JS, CSS, fonts) and the *shell* HTML (the SPA entry point).
  * For any uncached dynamic URL requested offline, serve a fallback `index.html` (or a special offline HTML page).
  * That fallback page boots your React app, which then uses client-side routing and cached/local data to render the page dynamically.

### 2. **Service Worker (Serwist/Workbox) configuration**

* Configure your service worker to:

  * Cache all static assets during install (`JS`, `CSS`, etc).
  * Use a `NetworkFirst` or `StaleWhileRevalidate` strategy for API/data requests, if possible.
  * For navigation requests (requests for pages), implement a `catch` fallback to your offline shell page.

Here’s a sketch for `sw.ts` with Workbox-like logic:

```ts
import { precacheAndRoute, createHandlerBoundToURL } from 'workbox-precaching';
import { registerRoute, NavigationRoute } from 'workbox-routing';

// Precache files injected by build process
precacheAndRoute(self.__WB_MANIFEST || []);

// SPA fallback to index.html for navigation requests
const handler = createHandlerBoundToURL('/index.html');

const navigationRoute = new NavigationRoute(handler, {
  denylist: [/^\/_next\//, /^\/api\//], // Don't fallback API or static assets requests
});

registerRoute(navigationRoute);

// Optionally add runtime caching for API calls here
```

Make sure `index.html` is in the precache manifest.

### 3. **Next.js config (`next.config.js` or `.ts`)**

* You may want to customize the output to ensure your SPA shell (`index.html`) is available for offline fallback.
* Using `output: 'export'` or custom serverless config could help generate a fallback page.
* However, with App Router, make sure to handle static fallback properly, which can be tricky since Next.js 13+ focuses on SSR/ISR.

There’s no official built-in Next.js config for Service Worker integration yet, so you typically add your custom `sw.ts` and integrate it manually or with plugins like `next-pwa` (which is working on App Router support).


### 4. **Data storage and hydration**

* Since users may request dynamic pages offline they haven’t visited before, you’ll need a way to hydrate those pages client-side:

  * Cache data responses (e.g., via IndexedDB or LocalStorage) when online.
  * Your app’s client components should read from this cache and render accordingly.
  * This requires custom logic in your React components to detect offline mode and fallback to cached data.

### 5. **Practical references**

* [Workbox Recipes - Offline Fallback](https://developers.google.com/web/tools/workbox/guides/common-recipes#offline_fallback) - general pattern for SPA fallback.
* [next-pwa plugin](https://github.com/shadowwalker/next-pwa)-check if their latest version supports App Router and dynamic fallback.
* Community examples for Next.js 13+ offline apps are sparse, but this thread helps:
  [https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/42273](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/42273)

### Summary

* Your approach is valid: pre-cache static assets + fallback HTML for navigation requests.
* Implement Service Worker to serve your fallback shell for uncached dynamic routes offline.
* Manage data caching client-side with IndexedDB/LocalStorage for offline hydration.
* Watch Next.js and PWA plugin updates for better App Router support.

Feel free to share your config and SW code here if you want feedback!

body:
Hi @jcald1,

This error usually happens because something in your build is trying to access `useContext` from React but ends up with a `null` value, often due to React version mismatches or incorrect imports during SSR (server-side rendering) in Next.js.

A few things to check and try:

1. **React and React-DOM version alignment**
   Your `package.json` shows `"react": "19.1.1"` and `"react-dom": "19.1.1"`, which looks suspicious since React's stable releases haven't reached v19 yet (current latest is around 18.x). This could cause compatibility issues.
   Try downgrading React and React-DOM to a stable version compatible with your Next.js version (e.g., `"react": "18.2.0"` and `"react-dom": "18.2.0"`), then run a fresh install:

   ```bash
   npm install react@18.2.0 react-dom@18.2.0  
   npm clean-install # or delete node_modules + package-lock.json and npm install  
   ```

2. **Next.js version compatibility**
   You're using Next.js 15.4.6 actually, the latest stable Next.js version at time of writing is 13.x (unless you’re on some canary release). Please double-check the Next.js version because an incorrect or pre-release version could cause strange build issues.
   If you meant `next` v13, that’s great. Otherwise, pin the stable Next.js version:

   ```bash
   npm install next@13.4.4 # or latest stable version  
   ```

3. **SSR and Context usage**
   The error references the `_error.js` page and the 404 page during prerendering. Sometimes, hooks like `useContext` break if they’re called outside of React component trees or during prerender.
   Check if you have custom `_error.js` or `404.js` pages that might be importing or using React hooks improperly. If so, make sure hooks are only called inside functional components and not top-level code.

4. **Clear caches and rebuild**
   Since you already ran `git clean -xfd` and deleted `package-lock.json`, try deleting `.next` folder manually as well to fully clear cache:

   ```bash
   rm -rf .next  
   npm run build  
   ```

5. **Peer dependencies warnings**
   React-related packages like `@radix-ui/react-*` and others might have peer dependencies tied to specific React versions. Mismatched versions can cause runtime issues.
   After downgrading React, check `npm ls react` to confirm only one React version is installed.

**TLDR:**
The main suspect is your React version being too high or incompatible. Align React and React-DOM versions with a stable release compatible with your Next.js version and clear build caches. Also, review any custom error or 404 pages for hooks usage during SSR.

Hope this helps! Feel free to share any updates or errors after trying this.

body:
Hey @jcald1,
This kind of `useContext` null error during **`next build`** (but not `next dev`) almost always means that something in your dependency tree is trying to use a React hook in a way that’s incompatible with how Next.js prerendering works in production mode.

Since you’ve confirmed you’re on **React 19** and **Next 15** (which are stable releases now), the issue is more likely coming from:

**Third-party packages that haven’t fully updated for React 19**

   * Libraries like `@radix-ui/react-*` or other UI components might still have some internals that break under React 19’s new behavior (especially with concurrent rendering and stricter hook rules).
   * Try temporarily locking to `react@18.2.0` / `react-dom@18.2.0` and rebuilding. If the error disappears, you’ve confirmed a package compatibility problem with React 19.

**Server vs Client component mismatch**

   * If a component is marked as a Server Component but uses a hook like `useContext`, it will fail during build.
   * For example, in Next 15, you must explicitly add `"use client"` at the top of any file that uses hooks. Even if it worked in dev, production build is stricter.

**Error page rendering during prerender**

   * Even without a custom `_error` or `404`, Next uses its own error page internally, and if a dependency it imports uses hooks in the wrong place, it can trigger this.
   * To debug, run:

     ```bash
     next build --debug
     ```

     and look at the stack trace to see which component is actually calling `useContext`.

**Steps you can try:**

1. Add `"use client"` to any top-level component that imports Radix or other hook-based UI libraries.
2. Temporarily downgrade React to 18.x to check if the issue is React 19–specific.
3. Check `npm ls react` to make sure there’s only **one** React version installed (no duplicates inside `node_modules`).
4. If confirmed to be a library bug, see if that package has a React 19 compatibility branch or update.

If this helps, marking it as an answer would be appreciated!

body:
Hi @hardik2047 

That message means Turbopack tried to generate the compiled file for the / page (it writes to .next/**/app/page.*) and couldn’t. In practice this usually comes from one of four causes:

Common causes → fixes

**1. Route conflict for “/”**

- You have more than one endpoint mapped to / (e.g., both app/page.tsx and pages/index.tsx, or app/page.tsx plus an API route.ts at app/page/route.ts).

- Fix:

  - Keep only one UI entry for /: app/page.tsx (or group variant).

  - Move API handlers under app/api/.../route.ts (not under app/page), and remove any pages/index.* if you’re using the app/ router.


**2. Duplicate/invalid files in app/page**

- Files like app/page.js and app/page.tsx, or a folder named app/page with its own page.tsx, can collide.

- Fix: Ensure there is exactly one of:

``app/page.tsx   // or .js/.jsx``

``and it has a default export.``



**3. Write-permission or lock on the build output**

- The .next (or .turbo) directory is read-only, locked by another process, or synced by tools (OneDrive/Dropbox/antivirus).

- Fix:
```bash
rm -rf .next .turbo
# On Unix/WSL, also:
chmod -R u+rw . && find . -type d -name ".next" -prune -o -type f -print >/dev/null
```
Close any watchers, disable AV sync for the project, and re-run next dev --turbo.



**4. Missing/incorrect Next.js install (shows as Next.js 0.0.0)**

- Turbopack can’t resolve next, so it can’t write the endpoint.

- Fix (choose your manager):
```bash
# npm
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm i next react react-dom
npm run dev -- --turbo
# yarn
rm -rf node_modules yarn.lock && yarn add next react react-dom && yarn dev --turbo
# pnpm
rm -rf node_modules pnpm-lock.yaml && pnpm add next react react-dom && pnpm dev --turbo
```
- Make sure you run from the project root and that package.json has:
```json
"dependencies": { "next": "14.x", "react": "18.x", "react-dom": "18.x" }
```

### Extra checks (if it still fails)

- **Monorepo:** ensure the app package itself depends on next and you run the dev script from that package.

- **Node version:** use Node ≥ 18.17 (or 20.x).

- **Disk/paths:** verify free disk space and avoid very long paths or read-only locations (e.g., OneDrive).

Hi @AbelSanzDev,

I’ve seen similar issues with Next.js where the browser doesn’t update with saved changes, even after disabling Turbopack. Here are some tips that helped me and others troubleshoot this:
1.	Clear browser cache and hard refresh
Sometimes the browser aggressively caches files. Try a hard reload (Cmd+Shift+R / Ctrl+Shift+R) or clear cache manually. Opening in Incognito often bypasses cache, which explains why it works there.
2.	Check for service workers
If your app or any dependency registers a service worker, it might cache old files. Open DevTools > Application > Service Workers and unregister any active workers during development.
3.	Restart the Next.js dev server
Stop and start your dev server. Sometimes HMR or Fast Refresh breaks and restarting fixes it.
4.	Delete .next folder
Remove the .next build cache folder and restart the server to force a full rebuild.
5.	File watcher limits on macOS
MacOS sometimes hits file watching limits that prevent Next.js from detecting changes. Try increasing those limits by running:
```bash
sudo sysctl -w kern.maxfiles=524288
sudo sysctl -w kern.maxfilesperproc=524288
```
Then restart your machine.

6.	Try a different package manager
Since you’re using pnpm, there might be issues with file symlinks affecting watchers. Test with npm or yarn to see if the problem persists.
7.	Check editor save settings
Some editors save files atomically or in a way that doesn’t trigger watchers properly. Try different editors or adjust save settings.

If none of these help, consider creating a minimal reproducible repo and sharing it here so the community can help debug further.

Hope this helps!

body:
Hey @adiranawal,
I ran into a very similar issue when building on Windows, and in my case it turned out to be a combination of **Next.js prerendering the `_error` page** and a **dependency (Radix UI in particular) importing `useContext` in a non-client context**.

A few things that fixed it for me:

### Ensure client components have `"use client"`

Next.js 15+ is stricter about when hooks like `useContext` can run.
If any of your components (or a dependency’s wrapper) calls hooks but is being rendered on the server, you’ll get this error.

**Check:**

```js
// Add this to the top of components that must run on the client
"use client";
```

For Radix UI components, you may need to wrap them in your own `"use client"` file, then import from that instead.

### Force consistent React & React-DOM versions

On Windows, I found that multiple versions of React were being resolved in `node_modules` due to peer deps.
Run:

```bash
npm ls react
```

If you see more than one, align them:

```bash
npm install react@19.1.1 react-dom@19.1.1
```

(or whatever single version you’re targeting)

### Check for stale `.next` cache on Windows

Sometimes the `.next` build cache stores server-side compiled versions of components from an older React version.
Delete it and rebuild:

```bash
rd /s /q .next
npm run build
```

### Test with `next.config.mjs` set to output standalone

This can help narrow down dependency inclusion issues:

```js
export default {
  output: "standalone",
}
```
**Why Vercel builds work but Windows doesn’t:**
Vercel runs on Linux, where the dependency tree may resolve differently and cached `.next` builds are isolated per build. On Windows, Next.js sometimes picks up cached, server-compiled artifacts or resolves different dependency entry points — causing SSR to break when `useContext` is called in a non-client render path.

After I marked my Radix imports as `"use client"` and ensured a single React version, the error disappeared both locally and on Vercel.

Hi @Devansh4971 

You’re seeing “Next.js package not found” (with Next.js version: 0.0.0) because Turbopack can’t resolve next from your project. Here’s a fast checklist that fixes it in almost all cases.

### Quick fix (pick your package manager)

**npm**
```bash
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json .next
npm install next react react-dom
npm run dev -- --turbo
```
**yarn**
```bash
rm -rf node_modules yarn.lock .next
yarn add next react react-dom
yarn dev --turbo
```
**pnpm**
```bash
rm -rf node_modules pnpm-lock.yaml .next
pnpm add next react react-dom
pnpm dev --turbo
```
### Things to double-check

**1. Run from the project root (the folder that has your package.json).**
Running next dev --turbo in a subfolder will produce this error.


**2. package.json must include:**
```json
"dependencies": {
  "next": "14.x",        // or the version you use
  "react": "18.x",
  "react-dom": "18.x"
}
```
(Don’t put next only in devDependencies for app runtime.)


**3. Node version**
Use Node >= 18.17 (or 20.x). Check with node -v. If needed, switch via nvm:
```bash
nvm install 20 && nvm use 20
```

**4. Monorepo / workspaces (TurboRepo, Nx, etc.)**

Ensure the app package (e.g., apps/web/package.json) has next in its own dependencies or is properly hoisted.

From that app’s directory, run the dev script:
```bash
pnpm --filter web dev --turbo
```
If using Yarn/PNPM workspaces, make sure nodeLinker/hoisting isn’t excluding next.



**5. Lockfile mismatch**
If the repo was installed with a different manager (e.g., pnpm-lock.yaml present), use the same tool. Mixing npm/yarn/pnpm often causes resolution failures.


**6. Corrupted install**
If errors persist, do a clean reinstall:
```bash
rm -rf node_modules .next
# remove the lockfile for your manager, then
corepack enable   # (for yarn/pnpm if needed)
<manager> install
```

**7. Bun**
If you installed with Bun, try running with Node once:
```bash
npm run dev -- --turbo
```
If it works on Node, the issue is Bun’s resolver—stick to Node for Turbopack.

body:
Hi @Dhavalkurkutiya 

This error means that Turbopack couldn’t locate the Next.js package in your project.
In the report, it shows:

**Next.js version: 0.0.0** → This usually means it’s not installed or not properly resolved.

**Error:** Next.js package not found → Turbopack is trying to load Next.js but can’t find it in node_modules or the project dependencies.


### How to fix it:

1. Check if Next.js is installed
```bash
npm list next
```
or
```bash
yarn list next
```
If it’s missing, install it:
```bash
npm install next react react-dom
```
or
```bash
yarn add next react react-dom
```

2. Make sure package.json has the correct dependency

```json
"dependencies": {
  "next": "14.x.x", // or your desired version
  "react": "18.x.x",
  "react-dom": "18.x.x"
}
```

3. Delete and reinstall dependencies

```bash
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json # or yarn.lock
npm install
```
(For Yarn: yarn install)


4. Run with Turbopack again

```bash
next dev --turbo
```

5. If still failing, ensure you’re running the command from the project root where package.json is located.


**This usually happens when:**

- You cloned a repo but didn’t install dependencies.

- The node_modules folder got corrupted.

- You’re running Turbopack from the wrong directory.

- The Next.js version is missing or incompatible.

---

**1. Next.js is not installed**

Check your package.json to see if next is listed under dependencies.

npm install next react react-dom

or, if you use Yarn:

yarn add next react react-dom

Sometimes the node_modules folder or the package-lock.json / yarn.lock file gets corrupted.

Try:

```bash
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
```
or

```bash
rm -rf node_modules yarn.lock
yarn install
```

---

**3. Invalid Next.js version**

In your screenshot, Next.js version shows as 0.0.0, which means the package wasn’t recognized.

Make sure you have a valid version in package.json, for example:

```json
"dependencies": {
  "next": "14.2.5",
  "react": "18.3.1",
  "react-dom": "18.3.1"
}
```

---

**4. Wrong command**

To start with Turbopack, use:

```bash
next dev --turbo
```

This only works on newer Next.js versions.

body:
Hey @Ryo98-SL  I can see this is a frustrating performance issue you're dealing with. Let me break this down in a way that hopefully makes sense.
So basically, what's happening is your browser is being a bit too "polite" - it's waiting for your CSS files to finish loading before it starts downloading your JavaScript chunks, even though it technically could grab them at the same time.

## Why This Happens 
Think of it like this: your browser is trying to avoid that awkward moment when a webpage looks completely broken for a split second. You know, when text is flying all over the place before the styles kick in? To prevent this, browsers have this rule where they make sure CSS is ready before letting JavaScript do its thing.
From your screenshots, I can see exactly what you're describing - those JS chunks are just sitting there waiting their turn while the CSS files are doing their thing. It's like being stuck in a really inefficient queue at the grocery store.

## What You Can Do About It
- Try preloading your most critical files with `<link rel="preload">` - this basically tells the browser "hey, I'm going to need this soon, start downloading it now"
- If some of your JavaScript isn't immediately needed, mark it as `async` or `defer`
- Consider inlining your critical CSS right in the HTML (just the stuff needed above the fold)

- Look into code splitting your CSS too, not just your JS
- Maybe explore CSS-in-JS solutions if you're using React or similar frameworks
- Check your bundler config - Webpack and similar tools have options for managing how chunks get prioritized
This is honestly one of those web performance gotchas that catches a lot of developers off guard. You're optimizing your JavaScript splitting (which is great!), but then CSS comes along and basically says "not so fast." 

The good news is that once you know what's happening, there are definitely ways to work around it. The screenshots from Perplexity and Claude's sites you shared show this is happening even on well-optimized sites, so don't feel bad about running into this.
Have you tried any preloading strategies yet?

body:
Oh nice catch by icyJoseph! That's actually a really good thing to check.
So basically, `fetchpriority` is like telling the browser "hey, this file is super important, grab it first" or "this one can wait, no rush."
**Here's what you should do:**
Just right-click on your page, hit "View Source" (or inspect element), and look for your CSS and JavaScript tags. See if they have something like `fetchpriority="high"` or `fetchpriority="low"` in them.

**What you're looking for:**
- Your CSS files might have `fetchpriority="high"` 
- Your JS chunks might have `fetchpriority="low"` or nothing at all
If that's the case, boom - there's your answer! Your browser is literally being told "CSS first, JavaScript later" and it's just doing what it's told.

or you can do is open Chrome DevTools, go to the Network tab, and look for a "Priority" column. You'll see things like "High", "Low", "Medium" - if your CSS shows "High" and your JS shows "Low", that's exactly why they're not loading in parallel.
This is probably happening because Next.js (or whatever you're using) is automatically setting these priorities, thinking it's being helpful by prioritizing styles over scripts.

body:
Hi @d-plz 

**Short answer:** that’s expected today.
The current “unstable” use cache APIs turn the segment into dynamic = 'auto', so they can’t be combined with dynamic = 'force-static'. Because the segment is no longer strictly static, you won’t get the same CDN/full-route caching behavior you get with standard fetch caching + ISR. The use cache memoizes function/component results at the data/function layer; it doesn’t yet synchronize 1:1 with the full route (HTML) cache.

### What to use right now

If your goal is: “generate /[slug] statically, cache it at both data and full-route level, and invalidate on-demand via tags/path,” prefer the stable path:

**1. Keep the route static:**

```ts
// app/[slug]/page.tsx
export const dynamic = 'force-static'; // or omit and ensure everything is static
export const revalidate = false; // use on-demand instead of time-based ISR
```
**2. Use fetch with cache tags:**

```ts
const data = await fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['post', slug] } }).then(r => r.json());
```
**3. In a server action or API route, trigger invalidation:**

```ts
import { revalidateTag, revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';

export async function invalidatePost(slug: string) {
  revalidateTag('post');     // data cache
  revalidatePath(`/${slug}`); // full route cache
}
```

This combo keeps the page truly static/ISR’d at the edge and lets you refresh both the data cache and the pre-rendered HTML on demand.

### When to try use cache

use cache is useful for memoizing expensive computations and composing caches inside components/functions, but it currently implies dynamic = 'auto'. Until it matures, don’t rely on it for ISR-style, CDN-level full-route caching.

**Bottom line:** For on-demand ISR with tag/path revalidation of both data and HTML, stick to fetch caching + revalidateTag/revalidatePath and a static route. Avoid use cache for this specific use case for now.
author: VictorMoni

body: Hey @victormoni yes that has been what I have been doing. You know if there is a more technical reason that prevented this being implemented while unstable? Like different signatures or something making it more difficult to integrate with force-static? Or this has been simply done deliberately since it's unstable as to not mess with full route cache for now?
author: d-plz

body:
Good morning @d-plz 

**Short answer:** it’s mostly deliberate while the API is unstable. use cache/unstable_cache introduces a runtime memoization layer at the function/component level, which can depend on request-time inputs. Because of that, Next has to assume the segment is dynamic: 'auto' instead of “truly static”, so it doesn’t couple it to the CDN/full-route HTML cache yet.

### Why that matters technically

**1. Determinism & safety.** A force-static route must be purely build/prerender-time. Once you allow use cache inside, that cache may depend on things like params, headers, or cookies (directly or indirectly). If Next kept the route static, you could leak personalized data into static HTML or poison the edge cache. Marking it dynamic avoids that risk.

**2. Two different cache layers.**

Function/data cache (what use cache manages)

Full-route (HTML) cache/CDN (what ISR + revalidatePath/revalidateTag target)
They have different keys, lifecycles, and invalidation semantics. Making them synchronize 1:1 requires dependency tracking across layers to prevent partial invalidation or stampedes.

**3. Build vs runtime pipeline.** force-static pages are produced during prerender/build. use cache populates at runtime. Mixing them would require warming/serializing function-level entries into the prerendered HTML and keeping those links consistent on invalidation—work that isn’t finalized.

**4. Dynamic promotion rules.** Next already promotes routes to dynamic when it detects dynamic signals (cookies(), headers(), no-store fetches, etc.). Allowing use cache to coexist with force-static would fight those rules and create surprising behavior.

**Net/net:** while use cache is unstable, it’s kept separate from ISR-style full-route caching on purpose. For on-demand ISR where you want both the data and the HTML refreshed, stick to a static route + fetch(..., { next: { tags } }) and invalidate with revalidateTag / revalidatePath. Use use cache mainly for memoizing expensive pure computations inside dynamic segments or server actions.

If/when the team lands cross-layer dependency tracking (tags flowing from function cache to route HTML) and a deterministic story for static output, these could converge—but today the separation is by design.

If I don't delete the `.next` folder, I will encounter this problem. I've tried many times, and this issue started happening after I switched from npm to pnpm.

I asked the AI, and its reply was:
---
This is a common issue when switching from npm/yarn to pnpm in Next.js v13/14.

Simply put, the problem lies in a conflict between the `.next` folder generated by `pnpm run build` and the development environment state required by `pnpm run dev`.

Running `build` creates a highly optimized production version inside the `.next` folder. When you then run `dev`, the development server tries to read this existing `.next` folder, but its internal structure and cache are designed for production, which confuses the dev server. As a result, it cannot find the modules needed in development mode (for example, the error mentioning `next/dist/pages/_app`, even if you are using the App Router, it might still check some old Pages Router paths in certain internal processes).

body:
Hi @Winfle 

It looks like the author is running into a core behavior of the Next.js App Router: as soon as you call headers() or cookies() in a Server Component (RSC/SSR), the framework marks the page as “dynamic” and sends it with Cache-Control: private, no-store. That means:

- You lose full-page public caching.

- The HTML can’t be cached by a CDN even if the only “dynamic” value is something that could be handled via Vary (e.g. accept-language).

- There’s no way today to explicitly say “I know this is safe to cache publicly with a Vary header.”


At the moment, there isn’t a built-in way to override this and keep public caching with HTML variants. If you truly need HTML to be cached with a Vary, the only supported workarounds are:

**1. Move the header/cookie handling to an API route**

- Render your page as static HTML.

- Use JavaScript on the client to call your API and fetch the variant-specific data.

- This keeps the HTML static (cacheable), but it means the variant logic happens client-side or via an extra request.



**2. Use Edge Middleware for variant handling**

- Middleware runs before the cache decision, and you can read headers there.

- You can then set Vary and route to different static assets based on the variant.

- This still has limits, because middleware itself doesn’t make the HTML dynamic — it selects which static variant to serve.



**3. Pre-generate variants as separate static paths**

- If the set of variants is small (e.g. languages), you can prebuild /en, /fr, etc.

- Then detect in middleware and redirect to the appropriate static variant.

- CDNs will happily cache each variant independently.


Unfortunately, there’s no public API in Next.js 13/14 that lets you call headers()/cookies() in a page and still tell the framework “this is public cacheable HTML with Vary” — the team would need to add an opt-in, like setCache({ mode: 'public', vary: ['accept-language'] }).

If you want this to change, the best path is to:

- Open or upvote an RFC in the Next.js repo proposing an explicit public-cache mode with Vary support.

- Provide your use-case (like you did here) to help the maintainers prioritize.
author: VictorMoni
imteekay

body:
This is a really good and valid point — Next.js’s current caching model treats any access to headers() or cookies() as dynamic, even when the data is not user-specific.
There should be a way to explicitly mark certain headers as public-safe and allow proper Vary behavior for CDNs.

A potential direction could be an API like:

export const dynamic = "auto"; // or "public-vary"
export const vary = ["accept-language", "x-customer-group"];


This would let developers signal that the page output depends on public HTTP variants, not private data.

Without that, as you mentioned, we’re forced to move logic into API routes just to preserve caching — which feels like a step backwards for performance and DX.

Hopefully the Next.js team considers adding a finer-grained control over caching boundaries and header-based variability.

That’s an internal Turbopack crash, often triggered by HMR (Hot Module Replacement) when a file changes during a build.

**Quick things to try:**

1. Stop the dev server and restart it (`next dev --turbopack`).
2. Clear `.next/` before restarting:

```bash
rm -rf .next
```

3. If it happens consistently after editing a specific file, try isolating the change — it might be hitting a bug in Turbopack’s incremental build.

Since this is an internal error (`turbo-tasks` effect instance missing), I’d recommend opening an issue with:

* Minimal reproduction repo
* Your OS + Node.js version
* Exact Turbopack + Next.js versions

For now, if you need to keep working, switch to Webpack (`next dev`) until the fix is merged.

body:
You’re right that Edge Requests will be much higher than users — **each file** (HTML, JS chunks, CSS, images, API/data, favicon, prefetches) counts as an edge request. \~40k/day for \~2k visits (\~20 req/visit) is not unusual, but you can often trim it.

**Things that usually move the needle:**

1. **Disable automatic prefetch where you don’t need it**
   Next’s `<Link>` prefetches route assets on hover/in-viewport and can multiply requests.

```tsx
// Per link
<Link href="/heavy-route" prefetch={false}>Heavy route</Link>
```

If you have many links (menus, footers, index pages), this alone can drop a lot of edge hits.

2. **Keep routes static (or cacheable) when possible**
   If a route reads `cookies()`, `headers()`, or sets `dynamic = "force-dynamic"`, it bypasses static/edge caching.

* Prefer `export const dynamic = "force-static"` or set a sensible `revalidate`:

```ts
export const revalidate = 60; // cache the HTML/data at the edge for 60s
```

* In `fetch()`, avoid `cache: "no-store"` unless truly needed. Use `force-cache`/`revalidate`.

3. **Check browser caching (to avoid repeat edge hits)**
   Your chunks show \~100% cache hit (good), but I notice `favicon.ico` often has low cache ratio in many setups.

* Put `public/favicon.ico` and send a far-future header:

```ts
// next.config.js
export default {
  headers: async () => ([
    { source: '/favicon.ico', headers: [{ key:'Cache-Control', value:'public, max-age=31536000, immutable' }] }
  ])
}
```

* Same idea for big, never-changing assets in `/public`.

4. **Reduce number of assets per page**

* Split “rarely-used” code with `next/dynamic` so it’s not loaded on first view.
* Audit third-party scripts and CSS.
* Use `next/font` (self-hosted) so fonts are cached efficiently.

5. **Images**

* Use `<Image />` with proper sizes and let Vercel cache them.
* If using many icons/images, consider sprite sheets or inlining tiny SVGs to cut requests.

6. **PWA layer (optional but effective)**
   A lightweight service worker that caches hashed `/_next/static/*` and `/public/*` can eliminate repeat edge requests for returning users.

**Is this expected?**
Yes: with modern apps, 15–40 requests per visit is common. What matters is **cache hit ratio** and **total transfer**. If most entries show high cache %, you’re in a good place; the raw “Edge Requests” number will still look big.

If you want, share a public route and I can point at the biggest request multipliers (usually link prefetch + dynamic routes + un-cached images).

body:
You’re hitting this because **Turbopack doesn’t support `esmExternals: "loose"`**. That flag was a Webpack-mode escape hatch and isn’t implemented in Turbopack.

**Fixes:**

1. **Remove it** from your config (recommended):

```js
// next.config.(js|ts)
export default {
  // experimental: { esmExternals: "loose" }, // ❌ remove
}
```

If you added anything under `experimental.turbo` before, note it’s **deprecated**—use the top-level `turbopack` key only for things Turbopack actually supports.

2. **If you rely on “loose” behavior**, run with Webpack instead of Turbopack for now:

* Dev: start without Turbopack (e.g. `next dev`, not `next dev --turbopack`)
* Keep `esmExternals: "loose"` only when using Webpack.

That should unblock the build. If you share a repro, happy to confirm which dep is requiring “loose” and whether there’s a Turbopack-friendly alternative.

body:
After talking with a number of customers about this issue, we've observed that this can happen for a number of reasons.

## Lack of Skew Protection

This is a legitimate issue. If you observe a spike in chunk load errors when shipping a new deployment, it's because you need to use skew protection.

The issue is basically that the user's browser is stuck on an older version of the app, so it's trying to request chunks that no longer exist. This is not simply a framework issue, but rather a general deployment platform issue. Every framework has the same problem. Many platforms support Next.js's implementation of skew protection which uses query parameters to differentiate deployment ids.

We highly recommend turning on *Skew Protection* for your deployment platform of choice:
- [Vercel Documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/skew-protection)
- [Cloudflare with OpenNext Documentation](https://opennext.js.org/cloudflare/howtos/skew)
- [Netlify Documentation](https://docs.netlify.com/build/frameworks/framework-setup-guides/nextjs/overview/#enabling-skew-protection)

## Aborted Requests or Flaky Network

There are good reasons a request for a chunk can fail that are not application or framework issues. This could be due to a flaky and unreliable network connection, or an aborted request when the browser begins navigating away from a page.

**Errors in this case are typically not an issue, and can be safely ignored.**

For the flaky network situation we have considered adding an optional equivalent of `webpack-retry-chunk-load-plugin`, ~but we don't have a timeline for this~ [*this will ship as on-by-default for Turbopack in Next 16.3*](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/94918). Chunk loading error semantics are a little messy and most frameworks do not retry chunk load errors.

## Differences in Sentry Filters (or other logging platforms, e.g. posthog)

If you have skew protection enabled, any remaining chunk load errors are often just noise. For this reason, Sentry has an option to filter these out.

![](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/44c8726d-67bb-4c39-9d45-bfc75c7bae7a)

However, we discovered that Sentry wasn't filtering out chunk load errors from Turbopack. For this reason, [we recently renamed the error we emit from Turbopack to match the name that webpack produces](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/86593). That change shipped with Next 16.1.

If you're on Next 16.1, have this option enabled in Sentry, and are still seeing chunk load errors in your Sentry logs, please [open an issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/new/choose).

Similarly, you may see these logs on other platforms such as posthog. If you've already enabled skew protection, you should be able to configure a filter for your logging platform to hide these low-value error messages.

Finally, if you can locally reproduce chunk load issues outside of this list of reasons, then please [open an issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/new/choose).

Hi @mtlaso ### PPR vs React's `use` API **PPR (Partial Prerendering)** in Next.js allows you to combine static and dynamic content in the same route, improving performance and SEO. The **React 19 `use` API** lets you consume Promises directly inside a component, simplifying data loading with `Suspense`. The example shown in the post can be rewritten to use the `use` API like this: ```jsx import { Suspense, use } from 'react' import { cookies } from 'next/headers' import { AvatarSkeleton } from './user' export const experimental_ppr = true export default function Page() { const session = cookies().get('session')?.value return (

My example with React's `use` API

}>
) } // "use client" function User(sessionPromise) { const session = use(sessionPromise) return
{session}
} ``` **Summary:** - **PPR** - mixes static/dynamic content, rendering part at build time and part on demand. - **`use` API** - declaratively consumes Promises, simplifying `Suspense` usage. ### References - [Next.js Partial Prerendering Docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/rendering/partial-prerendering) - [React `use` API RFC](https://github.com/reactjs/rfcs/pull/229) - [React Suspense Docs](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense)
author: VictorMoni

body:
Hi,

The key bit in your example is that, without PPR, every time Page is hit - you'd need to render the entire top-down tree. 

You can think of PPR as an enhancement that at build time, knows how to carve out the static shell, the bits that don't depend on the cookie, or dynamic behavior. The static shell boundary ends at the Suspense boundary. 

So with PPR on, at build time the shell is calculated and extracted, and then on every new request, or when prefetching a page, the shell can be reused, and then we only need to collect the dynamic bit, and in your case, that'd get streamed to the client interactive javascript, rather than waiting for the whole thing to render server side, or being streamed into RSC slots in the client.

body:
In **Next.js ≤15.4.x**, the `--turbopack` CLI flag is basically a shortcut for “turn on Turbopack mode” at runtime.
So that flag sets `experimental.turbo: true` under the hood. So even you didn't set it in your `next.config.js` file, that warning will be appeared. 
So instead of relying on `experimental.turbo` (old key), you should explicitly enable Turbopack in your config under the **new stable key**.
```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  turbopack: {
    root: __dirname, // optional
  },
};
```

And about second warning
```
⚠ Support for Turbopack builds is experimental.
```
Turbopack still isn’t fully stable.
That’s not about your config — that’s a general disclaimer from the Next.js team.
They still don’t recommend Turbopack for mission-critical production apps, but it’s getting closer.

To avoid this warning while keeping turbopack testing,

You can check the reference here: #78192 (comment).

In addition, the latest Next.js canary releases now indicate how many lock files are present and specify which one will be used.

OR:

This error happens because the Next.js package is missing or not installed correctly.

How to fix it:

**1. Install Next.js and React**
   ```bash
   npm install next react react-dom
   ```
   or with Yarn:
   ```bash
   yarn add next react react-dom
   ```

**2. Check your package.json**

   Make sure it includes:
   ```json
   "dependencies": {
     "next": "14.x",
     "react": "18.x",
     "react-dom": "18.x"
   }
   ```

**3. Clear cache and reinstall**
   ```bash
   rm -rf node_modules .next package-lock.json
   npm install
   ```

**4. Run in the correct folder**

   Ensure you are in the project root where `package.json` is located.

**5. Update Next.js if needed**
   ```bash
   npm install next@canary
   ```

In short: Reinstall Next.js in your project root and clear cache.

author: snebjorn

body:
Yeah, the reason webpack “works” but Turbopack fails is that `find-up@7` is ESM-only.  
When you do `require('find-up')`, webpack can patch it with `esmExternals: 'loose'`, but Turbopack doesn’t support that interop yet.  

That’s why `find-up@5` (CJS) works fine, while v7 throws the “server relative imports” error.  
The real fix is to switch your usage to ESM:

```js
// in ESM files
import { findUp } from 'find-up'

// in CJS
const { findUp } = await import('find-up')
You don’t really control Next’s output format (CJS vs ESM) — the key is making your own packages and imports ESM-friendly.
If you need a quick workaround: pin find-up@5 and later move to ESM when Turbopack’s interop improve

body:
**Context**
- Version: Next.js 14.2.23
- Env: Middleware (`middleware.ts`)

**Cause**
Middleware runs *before* the RSC pipeline and only allows request inspection and rewriting/redirects. Returning a `Response` with custom headers from middleware will short-circuit the RSC processing. That’s why you see the raw `RSC` payload instead of rendered HTML.

**Fix (minimum viable)**
1. Keep middleware minimal:
   ```ts
   import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'

   export function middleware(req: NextRequest) {
     return NextResponse.next()
   }
   ```
   You can still attach headers here, but avoid handling 304 logic.

2. Move Last-Modified / ETag / Cache-Control logic to:
   - A **route handler** (`app/api/.../route.ts`) or
   - A **custom server / edge function**.

   Example in a route handler:
   ```ts
   export async function GET(req: NextRequest) {
     const res = NextResponse.json(data)
     res.headers.set('Last-Modified', new Date().toUTCString())
     res.headers.set('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=60')
     return res
   }
   ```

3. If you need conditional 304:
   - Check `If-None-Match` or `If-Modified-Since` inside the **route handler**.
   - Return `new Response(null, { status: 304, headers })` there.

**Notes**
- Middleware can’t safely return `304` for dynamic pages, because RSC expects the full server response.
- Docs: [Next.js Middleware](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/middleware) and [Route Handlers](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/route-handlers).


If this solves it, please **Mark as answer** so others can find it.

body:
Hi,

I think the plan, as of today, for this use case is an API called `'use cache: private'`, you can find references to it in the code base - it is still under development - I personally haven't used it yet.

It is more an escape hatch for when you eventually can't do as you describe with regular `'use cache'` - the idea is to try and use `'use cache'` **_as much as possible, and only very rarely,_** **_if at all_**, apply the private cache.

There's no plan to allow `use cache` to access cookies/headers ~
author: icyJoseph

body:
It's cool there is a solution! May give it a try once ready.

However, I still find it confusing why private cache is an escape hatch rather that a default experience.
author: infodusha

body:
Right, they’re solving two different problems. The default “use cache” wants to be deterministic and maximize shareability. You can precompute with a small set of inputs and get maximum cache hits. Like you could derive locale to use, or dark/light mode from the cookie, and keep the variations small.

“use cache: private” is for per-user variability. It is a dynamic API explicitly, so you can wrap it in Suspense and still reuse work via a private cache. I notice now reading some code that headers are not allowed, only cookies though.

I think if private cached data is still fresh enough, the client router can include it in a runtime prefetch so the next navigation is instant too.

They also make it clear and explicit, so you know a private cache directive, is opting into dynamic behavior, whereas use cache, can be pre-rendered, just by reading the code. If things are implemented incorrectly, an error is raised.

I still need to refine how I communicate my mental model around these, but I think that's roughly the case.

body:
Looks like this is expected behavior.
`getConfig()` only works in a server context, so when you call it from `instrumentation-client.ts` it’ll always return `undefined`. That file runs on the client side, so runtime config isn’t exposed there.
If you need to access config values for Sentry setup, you have two options:
=> Move that logic into `instrumentation.ts` (the server instrumentation file).
=> Or, if the values are safe to expose, put them in `NEXT_PUBLIC_ ` env variables so they’re available on the client.

That should stop `getConfig()` from giving you `undefined` in the client instrumentation file.
author: priyanshusinghchouhan

body: So the publicRuntimeOptions that otherwise are accessible on the client and gotten from getConfig are not ok ro use here?
author: cupofjoakim

body:
Exactly — `publicRuntimeConfig` isn’t available inside `instrumentation-client.ts`.  
That file runs very early in the client lifecycle, so it won’t have access to runtime config.  

If you need something client-side, the safe way is to move it into `NEXT_PUBLIC_` env vars instead.  
That way it’s directly exposed and won’t rely on `getConfig()`.

Update Next.js to the latest canary (includes Turbopack fixes)

body:
This error usually happens because Turbopack cannot find the Next.js package in your project. The most common reason is that Next.js has not been installed yet. To fix this, check your `package.json` file and make sure that `"next"` is listed under dependencies. If it is missing, you can install it by running `npm install next react react-dom` or `yarn add next react react-dom`.

Another possible cause is a corrupted `node_modules` folder. In this case, you can try deleting the `node_modules` folder along with the lock file (`package-lock.json` or `yarn.lock`) and then reinstall all dependencies using `npm install` or `yarn install`.

It is also important to ensure that your project is running on a supported version of Next.js, since Turbopack is still experimental and requires Next.js 13 or newer. If necessary, update your Next.js version by running `npm install next@latest`. Finally, make sure that you are starting the development server from the correct directory, specifically the root folder that contains the `package.json` file.

In short, verify that Next.js is installed, reinstall your dependencies, upgrade to a supported version if needed, and run your commands from the proper project directory. These steps usually resolve the “Next.js package not found” error when using Turbopack.

body:
You’re hitting a known compatibility gap: **Turbopack doesn’t support Yarn Plug-n-Play (PnP)**. That’s why it can’t “find” the `next` package under PnP, and why things work either (a) when you switch Yarn to `node-modules` via `.yarnrc.yml`, or (b) when you turn Turbopack off. This isn’t a local misconfig—Next’s own docs explicitly say PnP isn’t supported with Turbopack. ([[Next.js](https://nextjs.org/docs/14/architecture/turbopack)][1])

### Practical alternatives (that keep Turbopack on)

Pick any one of these—no need to use `.yarnrc.yml` or `--turbo=false`.

1. **One-off env var (no repo config change)**
   Use Yarn with `node_modules` *just for this shell*:

```bash
# from your app workspace
YARN_NODE_LINKER=node-modules yarn install
yarn dev --turbo
```

Yarn allows overriding settings via env vars, so you don’t need a `.yarnrc.yml` file for this. ([[yarnpkg.com](https://yarnpkg.com/configuration/yarnrc)][2], [[GitHub](https://github.com/yarnpkg/berry/issues/2955)][3])

2. **Switch to npm or pnpm for this app (node\_modules linking)**
   Both use `node_modules` by default and work fine with Turbopack:

```bash
# npm
rm -rf node_modules .pnp.* .yarn/cache
npm i
npm run dev -- --turbo

# pnpm
rm -rf node_modules .pnp.* .yarn/cache
pnpm i
pnpm dev --turbo
```

(If you’re in a monorepo, run these in the app workspace so `next` is a **direct** dependency of the app.)

3. **Workspace-local config only (scoped)**
   If you want Yarn across the repo but only flip this app:

```bash
# in apps/your-next-app/.yarnrc.yml
nodeLinker: node-modules
```

This keeps PnP elsewhere while making this workspace Turbopack-compatible.

### Quick health checks (avoid common gotchas)

* Ensure `next`, `react`, and `react-dom` are **declared in the app’s `package.json`** (not just the repo root). Run: `yarn workspace <app> add next@^15 react@^19 react-dom@^19`.
* Run `yarn why next` to confirm the app resolves the real Next package (not a misnamed local workspace).
* Delete caches: `rm -rf .next node_modules .pnp.* .yarn/cache` then reinstall.
* Stay on **Node 20 x64** (you said Node 20—good). Some Windows reports blamed wrong Node arch; the fix was reinstall x64 and clean caches. ([[Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79458011/turbopack-issue-with-nextjs15-in-windows)][4])

### About the “Next.js version: 0.0.0”

That printout is a known logging quirk seen alongside canary Turbopack builds; it doesn’t necessarily reflect your installed `next` version. ([[GitHub](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/81849)][5])

---

**Bottom line:** There’s no supported way to run **Turbopack + Yarn PnP** today. Use node\_modules linking via a temporary env var, a workspace-local `.yarnrc.yml`, or switch this app to npm/pnpm—any of those will let you keep Turbopack on. If you still see “Next.js package not found” after moving off PnP, it’s usually project-root resolution or a Yarn 4/PnP residual—see similar reports and fixes in the Next issues. ([[GitHub](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/74226)][6])

body:
Right, so the question we need to answer is, why do barrel-files not make tree shaking just work?

Barrel files tend to be problematic because bundlers often can't prove that dropping some code is ok, because it was side-effect free. Mostly we see this problem with icon libraries, or libraries that pack a lot of utilities, for that Next.js has. way to rewrite the imports for you, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/optimizePackageImports, but it might be negatively be impact by side-effects.

Here's a thread that discusses barrel files: https://github.com/webpack/webpack/discussions/16863#discussioncomment-9374633

If you search around, you'll find many that say barrel files are anti-pattern. 

I think there's a way to get this to work but it is, IMHO, brittle. I rather use proper imports and not barrel files. Telling bundlers that things are sideEffect free, but maybe you can infer it from here, https://webpack.js.org/guides/tree-shaking/#mark-the-file-as-side-effect-free

~One other thing is that as that link says, in 100% ESM work it should just work - if I add `"type": "module"` - then it does drop it, with Webpack builds - I tested Turbopack and it didn't just yet.~ Nope I must have done something else... sorry about the misinformation.

Given all of this, one might as well just avoid the barrel-files - unless there's strong reason for it?

Agree, I faced all issues that you described before `typedRoutes` became stable, which made me search for other approaches at the time. 

What I found is that as soon as we have a dynamic route, it might not be as type-safe as you think. For instance, let’s say you have the following routes:

And you decided to change from `/items/add` to `/items/create`, you will notice that it will not throw any type errors for existing `/items/add` usage, as it can be considered as one of the `/items/[id]` routes

body:
I'm experiencing issu as well. The root cause is that Next.js generates catch-all routes in the `DynamicRoutes` type, which breaks type safety completely.

**Setup:** I'm using `[locale]/[...rest]` for i18n 404 handling with next-intl, a common pattern for internationalized apps.

**The problem:** When Next.js generates types for catch-all routes like `/${SafeSlug<T>}/${CatchAllSlug<T>}`, and `T` defaults to `string`, this evaluates to `/${string}/${string}`, which collapses `InternalRoutes` to `/${string}`, making all type checking useless.

```ts
type DynamicRoutes<T extends string = string> = 
  | `/${SafeSlug<T>}`
  | `/${SafeSlug<T>}/${CatchAllSlug<T>}`  // <- this is the problem
  | `/${SafeSlug<T>}/auth/login`
  // ... other routes
  ```

**Proposed fix:** Exclude catch-all route patterns from `DynamicRoutes` generation. Catch-all routes are typically used for 404 handling, not as navigation targets, so they shouldn't be in the typed routes union.

This issue is blocking typed routes support in next-intl (see [issue #396](https://github.com/amannn/next-intl/issues/396)), affecting a significant portion of Next.js users who need i18n.

**Workaround:** Manually defining routes works but defeats the purpose of `typedRoutes`.

body:
**Context**
- Windows 10/11
- Next.js 14.x with Turbopack
- Error: `failed to write ... .next\static\chunks\... (os error 1224)`

**Cause**
On Windows this error is almost always a *file lock*:
- OneDrive/Dropbox sync
- Antivirus/Defender scanning `.next`
- Editors holding file handles
- Deep project paths (NTFS + long paths)

**Fix (minimum viable)**
1) Kill stray processes:
   ```bat
   taskkill /f /im node.exe
   taskkill /f /im code.exe
   ```
2) Clean and reinstall:
   ```bat
   rmdir /s /q .next
   rmdir /s /q node_modules
   del package-lock.json
   npm ci
   ```
3) Move the project to a **short path** (e.g. `C:\src\next-app`) to avoid Windows MAX_PATH issues.
4) Exclude the project folder from **Windows Defender** or AV:
   - Docs: <https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-antivirus/configure-exclusions-microsoft-defender-antivirus>
5) Check permissions:
   ```bat
   icacls . /grant %USERNAME%:F /t
   ```
6) Rebuild:
   ```bat
   npm run build
   ```
   If it still fails, try:
   ```bat
   npm run dev -- --turbo
   ```
   or disable Turbopack temporarily:
   ```bat
   npm run dev
   ```

**Notes**
- This is a Windows-specific file lock, not a bug in your code.
- Docs: [Turbopack](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/optimizing/turbopack)

If this solves it, please **Mark as answer** so others can find it.

body:
**Context**
- Next.js 15 (PPR enabled)
- `<Link>` navigation reaches a page that should require auth
- It works on hard refresh but not on client navigation

**Why**
With PPR the shell can be prerendered and cached. If the auth check runs only on the client or the page is cacheable, the client navigation may reuse cached HTML and bypass your guard.

**Fix (minimum viable)**

1) **Enforce server-side auth check** in the page/layout and make it dynamic:
```ts
// app/(protected)/dashboard/page.tsx
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

// prevent caching of this route
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'        // or: export const revalidate = 0

export default async function Page() {
  const token = cookies().get('session')?.value
  if (!token) redirect('/login')
  return <main>Private</main>
}
```

2) **Mark your data as non-cacheable** if you fetch user/session:
```ts
await fetch('https://api.example.com/me', { cache: 'no-store' })
```

3) **Do not rely on client-only guards** (e.g. `useEffect` + redirect). They run too late for PPR and allow a flash or reuse cached shell.

4) Optional **edge gate** for global protection:
```ts
// middleware.ts at project root
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
export function middleware(req: Request) {
  const has = req.headers.get('cookie')?.includes('session=')
  if (!has && req.url.includes('/dashboard')) {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', req.url))
  }
  return NextResponse.next()
}
export const config = { matcher: ['/dashboard/:path*'] }
```

**Checklist**
- Protected routes: `dynamic='force-dynamic'` or `revalidate=0`
- Server check with `cookies()/headers()` + `redirect()`
- Any auth-related `fetch`: `cache: 'no-store'`
- Optional middleware for belt-and-suspenders

**Docs**
- PPR overview: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/rendering/partial-prerendering
- Dynamic rendering: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/rendering/server-components#dynamic-rendering
- Route middleware: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/middleware
- `redirect` and `cookies`: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/redirect , https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies

If this solves it, please **Mark as answer** so others can find it.

Thanks for bringing this up. What Joseph mentioned about `cacheComponents` and `dynamicIO` is spot-on, but to tie it back to your original problem:

When you use **PPR** with `<Link>` navigation, the redirect/auth logic can get skipped if the static shell is served without dynamic IO. That’s why the redirect might not trigger as you expect.

A couple of things you can try:

1. **Add logging** inside your auth/redirect function so you can confirm *when* it runs (prefetch vs navigation).  
2. **Enable `dynamicIO`** or combine PPR with `cacheComponents` — this ensures the redirect is respected even when the shell is cached.  
3. If possible, try a **minimal repro** with just the auth redirect + PPR. That helps confirm whether it’s config-related or something in your app logic.

In short: the fix is usually making sure `dynamicIO` is on and that the page/components are cached consistently. Otherwise the shell hits before your redirect runs.

Did enabling `dynamicIO` with `cacheComponents` solve the issue on your side?

body:
**Context**
- Next.js 14/15
- You ran `next build`, copied the project to a new folder, and built again
- Expectation: second build should be faster due to `.next/cache`

**Why the cache didn’t help**
The build cache is **path- and environment-bound**. When you duplicate a project:
- The **absolute project path** changes → cache keys no longer match.
- Tooling fingerprints include **Node version**, **OS**, **compiler binary (SWC/Turbopack)**, and sometimes **env vars**.
- `.next/cache` is considered an **ephemeral artifact**, not portable across machines or root paths. Copying it does not guarantee reuse.

**What to do instead**
1) **Don’t rely on copied caches.** Treat `.next/` as build output that can be deleted at any time.
2) For faster incremental builds, keep the **same project path** and environment between builds.
3) Ensure stable toolchain:
   - Same Node major (prefer Node 20 LTS)
   - Same Next.js version and lockfile (`npm ci` / `pnpm i --frozen-lockfile` / `yarn --frozen-lockfile`)
4) If you need repeatable fast builds in CI:
   - Cache your **package manager cache** (npm/pnpm/yarn), not `.next/`
   - Build inside the **same runner path** when possible
5) Local dev performance:
   - Use Turbopack in dev (`next dev --turbo`) for faster HMR
   - For production, expect a full compile on a **new path** even if `.next/cache` exists

**Notes**
- `.next/` contents are not meant to be checked in or moved across paths; they’re invalidated when fingerprints don’t match.
- Official build docs: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/next-cli#build

If this clarifies the behavior, please **Mark as answer** so others can find it.

body:
@samselikoff I think my case is similar. My desired behavior is to prerender/cache the entire shell of the page, but still fetch a small dynamic piece of user data (e.g. using Better Auth’s `getSession()`, which calls `headers()`).

Right now, if I add `"use cache"` at the page or layout level, I can’t call `headers()` deeper in the tree. I have to restructure everything to hoist that call out of the cached scope. That makes sense technically, but it’s painful in practice when only one small leaf component needs dynamic data.

Ideally, I shouldn’t have to worry about this. It would be great if we could wrap these dynamic calls (`cookies()`, `headers()`, etc.) in `<Suspense>` (or a `<Dynamic>` boundary?) and let Next.js figure it out: prerender/cache everything around it, but treat that subtree as dynamic and stream it.

I realize that’s probably complicated under the hood, but from a developer’s perspective it would massively improve DX. Right now it’s tough when you want to cache everything *except* one small piece that needs request data.

body:
Thanks for this - I'll put this in my stack of TODOs. Here are some thoughts on this matter...

> "auto no cache (default): Next.js fetches the resource from the remote server on every request in development, but will fetch once during next build because the route will be statically prerendered. If [Dynamic APIs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering#dynamic-rendering) are detected on the route, Next.js will fetch the resource on every request."
> 
> Either the documentation is inaccurate as it should also state that no cache does cache requests between next build commands, or this is a bug of sorts.

Right, this is problematic, because the next run, doesn't clean the cache (though `cleanDistDir` - true by default - does clean up other items). The purpose of the `.next/cache` folder is to reuse work already done.

> To improve build performance, Next.js saves a cache to .next/cache that is shared between builds.

In this case the statement `but will fetch once during next build because the route will be statically prerendered` - is not as useful as this other one, found here https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#fetch:

> [Static rendering](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering#static-rendering): Fetched data is stored in the [Data Cache](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#data-cache), and the rendered output in the [Full Route Cache](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#full-route-cache). Next.js serves this cached result until the path is revalidated.

Not that it is way better either, there's observable behavior here that we should communicate. **I'll see what I can do to surface this**. 

> force-static and no-store

Also agree here, we need to improve this bit.

When no-store is used, fetch is taken explicitly as a dynamic API, nearly equivalent to saying `await connection()` pre-rendering ends there.

When you override with `force-static` the pre-render pass w/ the outputs from `generateStaticParams` happens, and the fetch happens, and since it has no-store it is also not saved. 

This is a bit tricky to document I think - since it is something that `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` does to  `no-store` fetch requests, **perhaps this item belongs to the `force-static` section**.

---

Please do follow up if you think I've missed the mark - gotta get the facts right.

body:
The reason this doesn't exist is because if you used <Pagination> inside of a layout, then you'd need to refetch the layout upon every navigation.

`cookies()` and `headers()` exist because they're assumed to be static. They're stashed as if you read client cached data. And we know if cookies change because of `cookies().set(...)`. So neither are refetched on every navigation, but searchParams would have to be, which would cause layouts to re-render too frequently.
author: samselikoff

body:
Thank you for the explanation! That makes perfect sense.

I completely agree that forcing layouts to re-render due to `searchParams` changes would undermine one of the core benefits of the App Router, and the distinction you made between the highly dynamic nature of `searchParams` versus the semi-static nature of `cookies` and `headers` clarifies the trade-off very nice.

Given this, what are your thoughts on a more scoped version of this proposal?

Could a `searchParams()` function be introduced that is **explicitly disallowed or throws an error if used within a `layout.tsx` file**, but is available for use within a `page.tsx` component and its children?

The primary pain point of prop drilling exists *within* the page's component tree, not typically in the shared layout. A page and its children are *expected* to re-render when search parameters change.

This approach would:
1.  Solve the prop-drilling problem for page-specific components.
2.  Preserve the crucial performance and state-persistence benefits of stable layouts.

This seems like a way to get the ergonomic benefits where they are most needed, without compromising the architectural integrity of layouts.

What do you think about that?

body:
It looks like the issue is related to the **route structure in your `app` directory** when using Turbopack with Next.js.

The error:

```
Invalid segment Static("signup"), catch all segment must be the last segment modifying the path
(segments: [Static("api"), Static("auth"), CatchAll("nextauth")])
```

This usually happens when you try to define a **catch-all segment (`[...slug]` or `[...nextauth]`)** but then append another static segment after it. In Next.js routing, a catch-all must **always be the last segment in the path**, because it matches everything that comes after.

---

### How to fix

If your structure currently looks like this:

```
app/
 └─ api/
     └─ auth/
         └─ [...nextauth]/
             └─ signup/
```

This will throw the error, because `signup` comes **after** `[...nextauth]`.

You need to either:

1. Move `signup` before the catch-all, e.g.:

```
app/
 └─ api/
     └─ auth/
         └─ signup/
         └─ [...nextauth]/
```

2. Or, if `signup` is supposed to be part of the catch-all, handle it inside `[...nextauth]` instead of creating a new folder after it:

```ts
// inside [...nextauth]/route.ts
export async function GET(req: Request) {
  const { pathname } = new URL(req.url);
  if (pathname.endsWith("/signup")) {
    // handle signup here
  }
  // fallback to other nextauth logic
}
```

---

### Extra Debugging Tips

* Double-check your folder names in `/app/api/auth/`.
* Catch-all (`[...slug]`) **must always be last**. If you need more specific routes, put them **next to it**, not inside it.
* If you’re just setting up NextAuth, usually the correct structure is:

```
app/
 └─ api/
     └─ auth/
         └─ [...nextauth]/
             └─ route.ts
```

And you shouldn’t add extra static routes under `[...nextauth]`.

---

👉 In short: **Move `signup` out of the `[...nextauth]` folder, or handle it inside the catch-all.** That should fix the error.
author: TheusHen

body:
The error you’re seeing:

```
Failed to write app endpoint /page
Caused by:
- [project]/src/app/globals.css [app-client] (css)
- creating new process
- reading packet length
- unexpected end of file
```

This usually indicates that **Turbopack crashed while processing your CSS pipeline** (most likely inside `globals.css` or a PostCSS transformation). Because Turbopack is still experimental, these kinds of issues can show up when it tries to compile assets.

---

### Things you can try

1. **Check `globals.css` for syntax errors**
   Even a small typo (like a missing `}` or invalid CSS property) can cause the parser to fail. Try running:

   ```bash
   npx postcss src/app/globals.css
   ```

   to verify if it parses cleanly.

2. **Remove experimental config temporarily**
   If you have custom PostCSS plugins or experimental Next.js config in `next.config.js`, try disabling them to see if the error goes away:

   ```js
   const nextConfig = {
     experimental: {
       turbo: false, // disable turbopack fallback
     },
   };
   module.exports = nextConfig;
   ```

3. **Clear the `.next` cache**
   Sometimes corrupted build artifacts trigger this:

   ```bash
   rm -rf .next
   npm run dev
   ```

4. **Update Next.js / Turbopack**
   Since you’re on `Next.js version: 0.0.0` (probably nightly or canary build), make sure you’re on the latest commit:

   ```bash
   npm install next@canary
   ```

5. **Try without `globals.css`**
   Rename `globals.css` temporarily and see if the error disappears. If it does, the problem is inside that file or one of its PostCSS imports.

---

### Why this happens

* Turbopack is still **not production-ready**. Errors like *“unexpected end of file”* mean the bundler crashed while parsing assets (CSS in this case).
* The build system tries to spawn a process to handle the CSS, but the process ends before completing → leading to the *EOF* error.

---

### Suggested Fix

* Start by validating your CSS file.
* If the CSS is fine, disable extra PostCSS plugins and rebuild.
* If nothing works, run with **Webpack** temporarily until Turbopack stabilizes:

  ```bash
  npm run dev -- --webpack
  ```

---

👉 In short: **validate your CSS, clear cache, update Next.js, and disable experimental config if needed.** If the issue persists, you may need to stick to Webpack for now.

body:
Hello! This is a common OAuth configuration issue with custom domains. The problem typically occurs due to redirect URI mismatches between your Supabase configuration and production environment.

**Solution: Update Supabase Redirect URLs**

1. **Go to your Supabase Project:**
   - Navigate to Authentication → Settings → URL Configuration
   - Update the following URLs:

```javascript
https://yourcustomdomain.com

https://yourcustomdomain.com/auth/callback
https://yourcustomdomain.com/api/auth/callback
https://yourcustomdomain.com/auth/confirm
```

2. **Verify Next.js Environment Configuration**
Ensure your `.env.production` file has the correct URLs:

```env
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://yourcustomdomain.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=your_supabase_project_url
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=your_supabase_anon_key
```

3. **Update Next.js Auth Configuration**
In your Next.js auth setup:

```javascript
export const { auth } = createClient({
  supabaseUrl: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL,
  supabaseKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY,
  options: {
    auth: {
      flowType: 'pkce',
      autoRefreshToken: true,
      detectSessionInUrl: true,
      persistSession: true,
    },
  },
})
```

4. **Clear Browser Data and Test**
After updating Supabase settings:
- Clear browser cache and cookies
- Restart your Next.js production server
- Test the OAuth flow again

The initial error occurs because Supabase redirects to the configured URL, which doesn't match your custom domain until the configuration is updated. Once corrected, subsequent attempts should work seamlessly.

AFAIK, they can be anywhere, even library code, as long as Next.js can find the `use server` directive in the right place. At the top of a file, or inside an async function.

So, the only issue I can ever see, is if this code is in a library, and bundled `"incorrectly"`, for example the entire library code is put into one file such that the `use server` directive is not in the right place, or if the directive is dropped altogether. I guess one might have to use `transpiledPackages` or something like that for `some` library use cases. 

As far as placing it as you describe, there should be no problem, within your own project code it should always work.

body:
Hey @NishuRajput12  👋

You don't need Next.js if you're focused only on backend, but if you want to grow as a full-stack developer, **it's definitely worth learning**.

Learn React first (Next.js is built on top of it), then move to Next.js for features like routing, SSR/SSG, and easier full-stack projects.

Since you already know Node.js/Express, Next.js will feel familiar for the backend parts. Good luck!

Resources to get started:
- **React:** [freeCodeCamp's React Handbook for Beginners](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/react-for-beginners-handbook/) 
- **Practice:** [Build React projects](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/master-react-by-building-25-projects/) 
- **Next.js:** [Official Next.js Tutorial](https://nextjs.org/learn)
author: KhaledSaeed18

body:
> Is it necessary to learn Next.js if I'm already good with REST APIs and backend logic?

`necessary` is a strong statement, it depends really, a fullstack dev who can leverage Next.js. and through the React framework, the available ecosystem is valuable for business development. 

In general, there's a number of frontend frameworks/libraries, such as Svelte, React, Vue, and there are various full-stack, backend for frontend style, frameworks such as Remix, SvelteKit, Next.js or Nuxt, which give you a set of features commonly used to scale web apps. 

> Does Next.js help in becoming a better full-stack developer?

For sure, you can learn about caching, static generation and incremental regeneration, master the backend for frontend pattern, etc... 

> Should I focus on React first and then move to Next.js?

Not necessarily, but it is often good to have a roadmap or guidance. To draw a parallel, in mid 2010's, often people who jumped into
learning React, would instead spend a lot of time with CSS. 

Having a clear roadmap or guide to help you focus learning a given subject or technique is important. 

You can learn Next.js as you learn React. Without guidance, you might run into issues, and become frustrated at Next.js or React, whereas the problem might be HTML fundamentals, just to give an example.
